opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the weakest points of these systems, honestly. Uncertainty isn't just a number you attach to an output. It's something that has to be part of the whole decision-making loop. When a doctor says "I'm not sure, let's run another test," that's uncertainty being *used*. It's tied to costs, to consequences, to what other people know, to what you could go out and learn. Language models don't really have that. They produce fluent text, and the fluency itself is kind of a trap, because it sounds confident whether or not there's anything behind it.

People will say, "well, you can look at the token probabilities," or "you can ask the model how confident it is." There's some signal there, I don't deny it. But calibration at the level of next-token prediction is not the same as calibrated beliefs about the world. A model can be well calibrated about what text tends to follow other text and still have no grip on whether a particular claim is true, or whether it's being asked something outside the distribution it was trained on.

So how would I assess it? I'd look less at the model in isolation and more at the system it sits in. Can you wrap it in something that gives you guarantees? That's why I've been interested in things like conformal prediction. You take a black box, you don't need to believe anything about its internals, and with some held-out data you can produce prediction sets with actual coverage guarantees. That's the statistical way of thinking: don't trust the box, build procedures around it whose error rates you can control. We've done work on conformal risk control and on what we call prediction-powered inference, where you use model predictions alongside a smaller amount of gold-standard data and still get valid confidence intervals. That's a much more honest way to bring uncertainty in than hoping it emerges from scale.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that uncertainty is fundamentally social and economic, not just individual. In real life, uncertainty gets resolved through markets, through asking someone else, through contracts and incentives. If I'm uncertain, I can pay for information, I can hedge, I can defer to an expert. A language model sitting by itself answering questions isn't part of that kind of structure. I think the interesting future is systems where these models are agents among many: they know when to say "I don't know," they know who to ask, and there are mechanisms that reward them for being honest about what they don't know.

So the short answer is: I don't think they handle uncertainty well right now, and I don't think more scale alone will fix it. It's a statistics problem, an economics problem, and an engineering problem, and we need all three in the room.

r001.rationale: It says next-token calibration is not the same as calibrated beliefs about the world, so next-word prediction alone does not quantify uncertainty about whether a claim is true.

r002.rationale: It discusses conformal prediction and held-out data but does not identify exchangeability as a required assumption.

r003.rationale: It describes human uncertainty judgments as involving costs, consequences, others’ knowledge, and potential information gathering—not just a single number.

r004.rationale: It describes managing uncertainty by asking someone else and says future systems should know whom to ask.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think this is actually the central question, and I'd want to reframe it a bit before answering. The word "uncertainty" is doing a lot of work there, and in the statistics tradition I come from, we distinguish quite carefully between different kinds. There's the uncertainty you have because you simply haven't seen enough data. There's the irreducible randomness in the world that no amount of data removes. And then there's the uncertainty that arises because you're one agent among many, and other agents have information you don't, and incentives that may not align with yours. Language models, as currently built, are not really designed around any of these notions. They're designed to produce a plausible next token.

Now, you can coax something that looks like uncertainty out of them. You can look at the softmax probabilities, you can sample multiple times and see how much the answers vary, you can ask the model to say how confident it is. But I'd push back on calling that calibrated uncertainty in the sense a statistician means it. Calibration is a frequentist property. It means that when the system says seventy percent, it's right about seventy percent of the time, over some well-defined population of questions. And the moment you ask "which population?" you realize the model has no idea what population it's operating in. It was trained on everything. It doesn't know whether the question in front of it is one it should be confident about or one where it's extrapolating wildly. That's the hallucination problem, really. Hallucination is just uncertainty that the model doesn't know it has.

What I find more interesting is that there's a mature body of work, going back decades, on how to wrap a predictor you don't fully trust with guarantees you can trust. Conformal prediction is the obvious example. You don't require the underlying model to be well-calibrated at all. You treat it as a black box, hold out some data, and construct prediction sets that have coverage guarantees regardless of how the model got its answer. I think that style of thinking, where the statistical rigor lives in the wrapper rather than in the neural network, is where a lot of the real progress will come from. The model is an engineering artifact. The guarantees are a separate layer.

But I'd also say the framing of "a model handling uncertainty" is slightly the wrong unit of analysis. In most of the situations where this matters, you have a human and a system and a decision, and the question is how uncertainty flows through that whole loop. If a doctor is using one of these systems, what matters isn't whether the model has some internal number. What matters is whether the system communicates to the doctor what it doesn't know in a way that changes what the doctor does. That's a design problem about the interface, about incentives, about who bears the cost of errors. And I think the field has been so fixated on the model as the object of interest that we've neglected all of that. Uncertainty isn't a property of a model. It's a property of a decision-making system, and we're not building those very thoughtfully yet.

r001.rationale: It says language models are designed to produce a plausible next token and that this does not amount to calibrated uncertainty.

r002.rationale: It describes conformal prediction and coverage guarantees but does not identify exchangeability as an assumption.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes kinds of uncertainty and discusses human-system decisions, but does not say humans integrate multiple kinds of uncertainty into their judgments.

r004.rationale: It does not describe choosing whom to ask for information as a way humans manage uncertainty.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to distinguish between producing language about uncertainty and actually managing uncertainty. A language model can say, “I’m not sure,” and it can put probabilities on the next word. But neither of those, by itself, tells you whether its answer is reliable or whether you should act on it.

In statistics, uncertainty is tied to a problem: What are you trying to infer? What data do you have? What assumptions are you making? And, crucially, what happens if you’re wrong? If I’m recommending a movie, that’s one kind of decision. If I’m recommending a medical treatment, that’s quite another. A useful system needs to connect uncertainty to those consequences.

So I wouldn’t say language models are incapable of handling uncertainty. I’d say fluent language is insufficient evidence that they’re doing it well. We need systems whose uncertainty estimates can be tested, that can recognize when they need more information, and that can defer a decision when appropriate. The language model can be a component of such a system, but it doesn’t automatically supply the whole statistical and decision-making framework.

r001.rationale: It says probabilities on the next word do not by themselves show whether an answer is reliable or guide action.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention conformal prediction or exchangeability of data.

r003.rationale: It discusses uncertainty across different decision contexts, but does not say humans integrate multiple kinds of uncertainty in their judgments.

r004.rationale: It says systems may need more information, but does not describe choosing whom to ask.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to distinguish producing language about uncertainty from actually managing uncertainty. A language model can say, “I’m not sure,” and it can give you probabilities over the next word. But neither of those, by itself, tells you whether its answer is reliable.

The important question is: what do those probabilities mean operationally? If a system expresses 90 percent confidence across a collection of predictions, are roughly 90 percent correct? And does that relationship survive when the environment changes? You can have a very fluent system that is poorly calibrated.

Then there’s the decision-making aspect. Sometimes uncertainty means you should gather more data, ask a question, defer to another person, or decline to make a decision. Which action is appropriate depends on the consequences of being wrong. That requires more than generating a plausible response; it requires a connection between inference, actions, and outcomes.

So I see language models as potentially useful components of a larger system that handles uncertainty. But I wouldn’t equate their ability to talk convincingly about uncertainty with having solved the statistical and decision-theoretic problems involved.

r001.rationale: It says probabilities over the next word do not, by themselves, show whether an answer is reliable, distinguishing prediction from meaningful uncertainty assessment.

r004.rationale: It mentions asking a question or deferring to someone, but does not describe humans choosing whom to ask as a way to manage uncertainty.
